facts.statement: Shingopana is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod whose name means "wide neck" in Swahili.
facts.quote: Shingopana (meaning "wide neck" in Swahili) is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod from the Upper Cretaceous (late Campanian-early Maastrichtian age) Galula Formation of Tanzania.

facts.statement: Shingopana was a quadrupedal sauropod that grew up to 8 meters long, making it smaller than the average sauropod.
facts.quote: Shingopana was a quadrupedal Aeolosaurin sauropod that would have reached up to 8 m long when fully grown, smaller than the average sauropod.

facts.statement: Part of the holotype skeleton was discovered in 2002 by scientists from the Rukwa Rift Basin Project led by Patrick O'Connor and Nancy Stevens.
facts.quote: Part of the holotype, TZ-07, was discovered in 2002 by scientists affiliated with the Rukwa Rift Basin Project, which was run by Patrick O'Connor and Nancy Stevens.

facts.statement: The species Shingopana songwensis was officially named in 2017.
facts.quote: The species Shingopana songwensis was officially named in 2017.

facts.statement: The holotype fossil shows evidence of insect bore holes that damaged the remains shortly after the animal died.
facts.quote: The holotype was damaged by insect bore holes shortly after the animal died.

facts.statement: Remnants of a bulbous expansion on the cervical vertebrae likely helped to strengthen Shingopana's neck.
facts.quote: Shingopana instead had remnants of a bulbous expansion on the incompletely preserved cervical vertebrae, which probably helped to strengthen its neck.

facts.statement: Four incomplete ribs with flanged edges were found in the holotype, though their specific function remains unknown.
facts.quote: Four ribs have been preserved with the holotype, but none are complete. The ribs had flanged edges, but their function is currently unknown.

facts.statement: Shingopana fossils were found in the Upper Cretaceous Galula Formation within the Rukwa Rift Basin in Tanzania.
facts.quote: The holotype was discovered in the Upper Cretaceous Galula Formation of the Rukwa Rift Basin in Tanzania.

facts.statement: Shingopana coexisted with other sauropods like Rukwatitan and Mnyamawamtuka, various crocodiles, the mammal Galulatherium, and lungfish in its ecosystem.
facts.quote: It would have coexisted with the sauropods Rukwatitan and Mnyamawamtuka, the mesoeucrocodiles Pakasuchus and Rukwasuchus, the mammal Galulatherium, an unnamed notosuchian, an unnamed turtle, an unnamed theropod and two types of lungfish (Lupaceradotus and an unnamed genus).

facts.statement: Phylogenetic testing suggests Shingopana is more closely related to the South American Aeolosaurini family than to any African titanosaurs found to date.
facts.quote: Gorscak & O'Connor's phylogenetic testing suggest Shingopana is more closely related to the South American titanosaur family of Aeolosaurini than any of the titanosaurs found so far in North & South Africa.

facts.statement: Shingopana was classified within the Aeolosaurini group as early as 2011, before the genus was officially named.
facts.quote: Shingopana se ha clasificado dentro de Aeolosaurini ya en 2011, antes de que se le diera un nombre al animal.

facts.statement: Shingopana belongs to the unranked family Titanosauria.
The parent group for Shingopana is Lithostrotia.
The time range for Shingopana is estimated from the Cenomanian to the Campanian, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Campanian (100.5 to 72.2 million years ago)
